title: Is Indian Manufacturing's Moment Finally Here? The Data Is Mixed
excerpt: The Economist says Indian industry is having its moment — but factory surveys, PLI payout data, and value-addition figures paint a more complicated picture.
body:
• The Economist argued this week that Indian manufacturing's moment may finally have arrived, citing the China-plus-one shift and the government's industrial push.
  • Factory activity supports part of the case: HSBC's manufacturing PMI rose to 55.1 in September, a seven-month high, on the strongest new-order growth since February.
  • But India's flagship production-linked incentive scheme has paid out only Rs 36,754 crore of the Rs 1.97 lakh crore announced — under a fifth — and generated 14.57 lakh jobs against a 60-lakh target, per commerce-ministry data.
  • What it means for you: for investors, be selective — electronics assembly is booming, but batteries, solar, steel and textiles lag; manufacturing-themed exposure now hinges on a handful of sectors.

The Economist argued this week that Indian manufacturing's moment may finally have arrived. On the surface, the timing looks right: factories are humming, exports are picking up, and global companies keep talking about China-plus-one. But a closer look at the government's own numbers tells a more sobering story — one of missed payout targets, stalled job creation, and value addition that never materialized.

The bull case: factories are humming

The strongest evidence comes from the factory floor. HSBC's India Manufacturing PMI, compiled by S&P Global, climbed to 55.1 in September from 52.8 in August — a seven-month high and a sharp rebound from August's five-year low, according to Reuters. Any reading above 50 signals expansion.

New orders rose at the fastest pace since February, driven by electronic, food, pharmaceutical and textile products. Export orders accelerated, with manufacturers citing increased demand from clients in Brazil, Europe, the UAE and the United States. Output growth was the strongest since May, employment expanded at its fastest rate since May after August's outright decline — the first drop in factory jobs in two and a half years — and business confidence hit a four-month high.

"The honest reading, for investors and NRIs watching India as a portfolio bet, is that the "moment" is sectoral, not national."

HSBC's chief India economist Pranjul Bhandari noted that companies were buying materials and building stocks ahead of anticipated sales, a sign of genuine demand rather than inventory noise. The macro backdrop helps too: India attracted over $70 billion in foreign direct investment in FY2025, as FDI policy reforms took hold.

The PLI reality check

But the centerpiece of India's manufacturing ambition — the production-linked incentive scheme — is where the story wobbles. An audit of commerce-ministry figures by The Core found that across 14 PLI schemes worth Rs 1.97 lakh crore, covering phones, cars, medicines, textiles, steel, solar, batteries and drones, the government had disbursed just Rs 36,754 crore by June 30, 2026. That is 18.7% of the announced amount, or 19.2% against the Rs 1.91 lakh crore actually approved.

The payouts are also heavily concentrated. Phone and finished electronics drew Rs 19,091 crore of a Rs 40,995 crore allocation; pharmaceuticals got Rs 6,662 crore of Rs 15,000 crore; food processing took Rs 3,271 crore. Those three sectors account for 79% of all money paid out. Everywhere else is a rounding error: cars and auto parts Rs 3,174 crore of roughly Rs 26,000 crore, white goods Rs 593 crore of Rs 6,238 crore, speciality steel Rs 236 crore of Rs 6,322 crore, medical devices Rs 157 crore of Rs 3,420 crore. Batteries and solar received nothing.

Some schemes look close to broken. The battery program set aside Rs 18,100 crore in 2021 for 50 GWh of cell capacity by 2025; by October 2025 only 1.4 GWh had been built, all by Ola Electric, Hyundai walked away from its 20 GWh share, and the heavy industries ministry has now given Ola and Reliance until 2031. The IT hardware scheme had its budget raised from Rs 7,350 crore to Rs 17,000 crore after poor uptake — and has still paid out only about Rs 98 crore. Textiles, despite three application rounds and repeatedly relaxed targets, paid Rs 386 crore, under 4% of its Rs 10,683 crore.

The jobs and value-addition gap

Two numbers matter most for whether this is a real industrial takeoff or a subsidy story. On jobs: the schemes created 14.57 lakh direct and indirect jobs by June 30, 2026, against the finance minister's February 2022 Budget projection of 60 lakh. On value addition: the government's own estimate puts domestic value-add in electronics at 18-20% — the electronics secretary's latest count is 22-23% — versus the 35-40% expected by FY26 when the scheme began. In other words, India is assembling more phones than ever, but the high-value components still come from abroad. The country imports over 85% of its crude oil and $24 billion of semiconductors a year.

Even the government has quietly moved the goalposts. The long-standing target of raising manufacturing to 25% of the economy — set first for 2022, then 2025 — is now described by the commerce minister as a 2047 ambition.

What's next

None of this means the manufacturing push is dead. The Cabinet approved a Rs 62,500 crore successor to the phone scheme, which ended on March 31, 2026, and the February Budget raised the components scheme to Rs 40,000 crore — though only Rs 1,500 crore is budgeted for it this year. Electronics assembly is genuinely scaling, export order books are filling, and the PMI trend is encouraging.

The honest reading, for investors and NRIs watching India as a portfolio bet, is that the "moment" is sectoral, not national. Manufacturing-themed exposure rides on electronics, pharmaceuticals and food processing — the three sectors that actually got paid. The rest of the industrial map is still waiting for its incentives to turn into factories.
